# Architecture

- ARC-004: Microservices, Blazor Hybrid for MAUI, and a non-LTS .NET target each need an ADR.
- ARC-006: Plans cover the five Well-Architected pillars (reliability, security with a short threat model where data or sign-in is touched, cost, operational excellence including observability, performance), plus accessibility, data and docs.
- ARC-009: Give an app only the structure today's requirements need: a web app starts with one ARC-001 module and gets another only for a second distinct business area (its own language, data and rules), never one per entity or feature; a console tool, a standalone worker or a library is one project and its tests, its concerns kept apart by namespace, until code another app must share or a boundary the compiler must enforce needs a second project (ARC-010 settles MAUI and desktop apps); every project, each of a module's five included, is created with its first real type, never before; and inside a module, aggregates, value objects, domain events, CQRS, a mediator, a generic repository or an interface that inverts no dependency come only with the requirement the plan names for each.
- ARC-012: Every tool, service and tier an app uses starts on the industry-standard option while it's free for the app's use; the new-app intake asks for a monthly budget, $0 when unanswered, and within that budget a plan picks the option that fits best; a paid option is always listed with its estimated price, the price's source and the date checked, never dropped; and spending money still needs the owner's OK (SEC-003).
- ARC-013: Every repo keeps a Mermaid diagram of its modules and the dependencies between them in docs/architecture/modules.md, updated in the same PR as a change that adds a module, a project or a dependency.
- ARC-019: Justify every design decision with a business requirement, and avoid over-engineering as well as under-engineering. Don't use CQRS and DDD patterns everywhere.
